newsitem.title: UK: T-bill liberalisation could boost Russia's appeal.
newsitem.headline: T-bill liberalisation could boost Russia's appeal.

text.p: Russia's decision to liberalise its domestic government bond market by the end of 1997 could boost the appeal of the country for foreign investors and lead to lower yields in the sector, bankers said on Monday.

"It will reduce borrowing costs, it will create a more efficient domestic market and increase Russia's access to capital, and these are all credit events," Eric Fine, Russia and eastern Europe debt strategist at Morgan Stanley in London, said.
"Brady's should not rally on this specific news, but by the end of the year events like these could end up being a rating event and having a very big impact on the market," Fine said.

Russia's central bank set a timetable on Monday which will gradually open up the rouble-denominated GKO discount Treasury bills or OFZ interest-bearing government bond market to non-resident investors by the end of this year, with the first change starting in May.
"From January 1 (1998) a foreigner can put in money and two days later, say, take it out," deputy chairman of Russia's central bank Alexander Potyomkin said in Moscow earlier.
Yields on Russian T-bills are higher than those paid on foreign Russian debt, like dollar-denominated Eurobonds.
On an annualised basis Russia's dollar Eurobond yields 9.93 percent, dealers said. Using available forward contracts to obtain dollar returns, T-bills offer an annualised yield of over 15 percent.
An economist at a European bank said Russia's desire to pay less for money borrowed on the domestic market was behind the changes which will allow foreign investors to buy and sell T-bills freely.
"Russia's intention is to get lower yields, and this is the reason they have opened up the market more quickly than expected," the economist said.

"(But) as long as Russia's political and economic situation remains at it is now, I do not expect any drastic moves in yields. The market needs more news in order to change its perception of Russia," he said.
Fine at Morgan Stanley was more positive.

"The changes are definitely faster than what the market was expecting, and the impact will be generally positive. Increasing foreign access to the local markets should reduce yields over time," he said.
Russia is rated Ba2 by Moody's Investors Service and BB minus by Standard & Poor's, putting it into the high speculative grade category.
